0.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
0.essay:
Every honest Christian knows the struggle. We love Christ and want to please him, and yet we keep falling into the same sins: a sharp tongue, a lustful look, a jealous thought, a habit we have confessed a hundred times.

Two wrong turns

Some Christians despair, wondering whether they are really saved. Others give up the fight and make peace with their sin. Neither is the Bible’s way.

Realistic and hopeful

Scripture is realistic. It never pretends that Christians are sinless in this life: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). But it is also hopeful. Sin no longer rules the believer. The Spirit lives in us. Christ has broken sin’s power, and one day he will remove its presence altogether. In between, there is a real fight, and it is a fight we are equipped to win.

Not a list of techniques

This study is not a list of techniques. The battle against sin is won by grace, through union with Christ, by the power of the Spirit, using the means God has given. But it is a battle, and it requires effort, honesty, wisdom and the help of other believers.

The chapters

Why Christians Still Sin; Dead to Sin, Alive to God; How Temptation Works; Putting Sin to Death; Fighting Together; and When You Fall. The study belongs with the studies on the Holiness of God and on Forgiveness and Reconciliation.

1.title: Why Christians Still Sin
1.essay:
When we become Christians, we are forgiven, justified and adopted. We are given new hearts and the Holy Spirit. So why do we still sin?

Remaining, not reigning

At conversion sin’s rule is broken: “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). But sin’s presence remains. Paul calls it the flesh — the old sinful nature that still clings to us and fights the Spirit. “For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other” (Galatians 5:17). Every believer has a civil war inside. Believers have new hearts, but the old nature has not yet been removed. We are new people with old habits, and sanctification is the process of becoming in practice what we already are in Christ.

Yet Paul does not leave the war as a stalemate: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). The flesh is still present, but it need not win.

The struggle is a sign of life

Paul describes the inner conflict with painful honesty: “For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate” (Romans 7:15). He traces it to “sin that dwells within me”, yet he also says, “I delight in the law of God, in my inner being” (Romans 7:22). His cry — “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” — is the cry of every believer who feels sin’s pull. And the answer comes at once: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

Before conversion most people do not struggle much with sin; they simply follow their desires. The fact that you hate your sin and fight it is evidence that the Spirit is at work in you. Dead people do not struggle.

A young Christian is shocked to find that after his conversion he still struggles with anger. He wonders whether his faith was real. An older believer tells him, “The fact that you are troubled by it is a good sign. Before, you would not have cared.” He begins to fight his anger with hope instead of despair.

Who is Romans 7 about?

Some read Romans 7:14–25 as Paul describing his life before conversion, or someone under conviction trying to keep the law in his own strength. Others read it as the normal experience of a mature believer who delights in God’s law but still finds sin at work in him.

Paul is describing his life as a believer. He uses the present tense throughout. He delights in God’s law in his inner being, which no unregenerate person does: “the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law” (Romans 8:7). And the passage ends not in despair but in thanksgiving. Romans 7 is not a picture of defeat but of the honest struggle of every believer, which Romans 8 then answers with the power of the Spirit.

Sin is deceitful

Sin never presents itself honestly. It promises pleasure, freedom or relief and hides its cost. It makes excuses: “Just this once.” “No one will know.” “You deserve it.” “It’s not that bad.” Hebrews warns, “But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). Sin deceives gradually, and the heart hardens slowly. Part of fighting sin is learning to see through its lies, and we need others to help us.

The world and the devil

Sin is not only within us. We live in a world that celebrates what God forbids, and we face a real enemy: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). The flesh, the world and the devil work together.

David was a man after God’s own heart, who wrote psalms of deep devotion. Yet he committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged her husband’s murder (2 Samuel 11). His fall warns that no believer is beyond the reach of temptation.

Honest, not pretending

John rules out two errors. Some claim to have no sin, and deceive themselves. Others claim never to have sinned, and make God a liar. The honest Christian admits his sin and confesses it, and finds God “faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Pretending to be sinless is far more dangerous than admitting we are not.

Until glory

The fight will last until glory; no Christian reaches sinless perfection in this life. But it is not hopeless. Sanctification is real and progressive. A Christian who has walked with God for forty years should be more like Christ than when he began, even though he will feel his sin more keenly than ever.

Here is a simple test: do you hate your sin, or only its consequences? Hatred of sin itself is a mark of the Spirit.

For reflection

What is the difference between sin remaining and sin reigning in a believer? Read Romans 7:14–25: where do you recognise your own experience? What lies does sin most often tell you? How does your struggle against sin show that the Spirit is at work in you?

2.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
2.essay:
The fight against sin begins not with what we do but with who we are in Christ. Paul’s great chapter on holiness, Romans 6, does not start with commands. It starts with facts.

Shall we go on sinning?

Paul anticipates an objection. If grace abounds where sin increases, should we keep sinning? His answer is horror: “By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” (Romans 6:2). Baptism signifies our union with Christ in his death and resurrection. Continuing in sin is not only wrong; it contradicts who we are.

We died with Christ

“We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin” (Romans 6:6). When Christ died, believers died with him. The old self — the person we were in Adam, enslaved to sin — has been put to death, and sin’s claim on us has been cancelled.

We were raised with him

We were buried with him “in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). We share Christ’s resurrection life now. We are new creations (2 Corinthians 5:17), and the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in us.

Consider yourselves dead to sin

Only after stating these facts does Paul give his first command: “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11). This is not pretending. It is believing what is true. Many Christians fight sin as if they were still its slaves. Paul says: you are free. Live like it.

Then come the practical commands: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions” (Romans 6:12). Do not present your members to sin; present yourselves to God as instruments for righteousness. Sin is a deposed tyrant still shouting orders, and believers do not have to obey. And underneath it all is the promise: sin will not be your master, because you are under grace (Romans 6:14).

A woman who struggles with gossip has always fought it by trying harder not to talk. Studying Romans 6, she begins each morning by reminding herself: “I died with Christ. I am alive to God. My tongue belongs to him.” She still fails at times. But her fight now starts from freedom, not fear.

Set your minds above

Colossians follows the same pattern: “If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:1–3). One day he will appear, and we will appear with him in glory. Setting our minds on these things is not escapism; it is the power for holiness, because what we love most shapes how we live. The way to fight earthly desires is to fill our minds with heavenly realities: Christ’s love, his glory, his return and our future with him.

Controlled by love

“For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). The motive for holiness is not fear but gratitude to the one who died and rose for us.

Facts before commands

Throughout the New Testament, commands rest on facts. “For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8). Because you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above. The order matters. Commands without the gospel crush us. The gospel without commands leaves us passive. Together they transform.

Sanctification has two sides. Definitively, believers have been set apart once for all as God’s holy people, and sin’s dominion has been broken. Progressively, they are being made holy day by day. The first guarantees the second. And everything flows from union with Christ: we died with him, were raised with him, are hidden in him and will appear with him. Sanctification is not a self-help project but the life of Christ in us.

Learning to live free

The Israelites, freed from slavery in Egypt, kept wanting to go back. They even said, “Let us choose a leader and go back to Egypt” (Numbers 14:4). Freedom takes time to sink in. Believers too must learn to live as the free people they are. Holiness is not trying to become someone we are not. It is becoming in practice who we already are in Christ.

When you fight sin, do you begin with “I must try harder,” or with “In Christ I am free”?

For reflection

What does it mean that your “old self was crucified” with Christ? Why does Paul state facts before he gives commands? How could you “set your mind on things above” in a moment of temptation? Write down one sin you struggle with. How does Romans 6:11 speak to it?

3.title: How Temptation Works
3.essay:
Understanding how temptation works helps us resist it, and Scripture gives a clear picture.

It begins within

“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death” (James 1:14–15). James describes a process: desire, enticement, conception, birth, growth, death. Our own desires lure us like bait. The fruit of sin is death, and its root is our own desire. The best time to resist is at the beginning, before desire conceives.

We cannot blame God: “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). Nor can we lay all the blame on circumstances or other people.

The first temptation

In Eden the serpent began by questioning God’s word: “Did God actually say, ‘You shall not eat of any tree in the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). Then he flatly denied God’s warning and slandered God’s character, suggesting that God was holding back something good (Genesis 3:4–5). Then the woman “saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise” (Genesis 3:6). She ate, and gave some to her husband, who was with her. Temptation still works this way. It doubts God’s word, distrusts God’s goodness and makes sin look attractive.

How Jesus resisted

Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness and tempted after forty days of fasting: to satisfy his hunger, to test God, and to gain the world by worshipping Satan. Each time he answered from Scripture, from Deuteronomy: “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). He did not argue with the devil or rely on his feelings. He held to God’s word. Where Adam fell in a garden with every provision, and Israel failed in the wilderness, Jesus stood in a wilderness with none. His victory is ours by faith, and his method is our model.

Temptation is not sin

Jesus “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Feeling the pull of temptation is not the same as sinning. The sin comes when we entertain, welcome and act on the desire. That is a great comfort to sensitive consciences.

A way of escape

“Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:12–13). Paul warns the overconfident and comforts the fearful. No temptation is unique to you. None is irresistible. And God always provides a way out. Often it is simple: leave the room, close the app, call a friend, pray. Pride is dangerous; despair is unnecessary.

Know your weak points

Temptation often comes when we are hungry, angry, lonely or tired. Jesus was tempted when he was hungry. David fell when he stayed idle at home while his army was at war (2 Samuel 11:1). Knowing our vulnerable moments helps us prepare.

A man notices that he is most tempted to look at pornography late at night, when he is tired and alone with his phone. He decides to charge his phone outside the bedroom and go to bed at a set time, and he tells a trusted friend. The temptation does not disappear, but the moments of greatest weakness are guarded.

Resist and pray

Satan is real and active, but not all-powerful. He cannot force a believer to sin. “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). He is a defeated enemy (Colossians 2:15).

Jesus taught us to pray, “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). Prayer is not a last resort but a first line of defence. In Gethsemane he told his disciples, “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). They slept, and fell.

Joseph ran

Joseph was tempted day after day by Potiphar’s wife. He refused: “How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). When she grabbed him, he ran, leaving his cloak in her hand. He saw sin as an offence against God, and he did not linger.

When are you most vulnerable to temptation? What is one practical step you could take to guard that moment?

For reflection

Trace the steps of temptation in James 1:14–15: where is it easiest to resist? How does the serpent’s strategy still work today? Which verses could you memorise to answer your most common temptations, as Jesus did? What “way of escape” does God most often provide for you?

4.title: Putting Sin to Death
4.essay:
The Bible’s language for fighting sin is violent. “Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5). Sin is not a pet to be managed but an enemy to be killed.

Radical measures

Jesus takes the seventh commandment to the heart: lustful looking is adultery of the heart. Then he says, “If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29). This is not a call to self-harm; it is hyperbole. But its point is deadly serious. Better to lose something precious than to lose your soul. Radical sin requires radical measures.

Paul lists the sins to put to death, beginning with sexual sins and ending with covetousness, which he calls idolatry, and then the sins of speech to put away. The reason: believers “have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:9–10). Holiness is the restoration of God’s image in us.

By the Spirit

“For if you live according to the flesh you will die, but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:13–14). We do the putting to death, but we do it by the Spirit. We cannot do it in our own strength, and the Spirit does not do it without us. Grace does not make us passive; it makes us active. And the fight itself is evidence of adoption.

Put off and put on

Paul’s method is not just removal but replacement. Believers are taught “to put off your old self … and to put on the new self” (Ephesians 4:22, 24). The thief should not merely stop stealing but work and give to those in need (Ephesians 4:28). The liar should not merely stop lying but speak the truth (Ephesians 4:25). An empty heart will soon be filled with sin again. A heart filled with love for Christ crowds sin out.

A woman struggles with envy whenever she looks at friends’ lives on social media. She deletes the apps from her phone for a season, and in their place starts writing down three things she is thankful for each evening. Over months, envy weakens and gratitude grows. She has put off and put on.

Flee

Some sins should not be fought but fled. “So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace” (2 Timothy 2:22). “Flee from sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Wisdom does not stand near the edge of a cliff to prove it will not fall.

Make no provision

“But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires” (Romans 13:14). Do not plan for sin. Remove what feeds it: the websites, the company, the habits, the hidden stash.

When the Ephesians turned to Christ, many who had practised magic brought their books and burned them publicly — books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). They did not keep them in a drawer just in case. Repentance was decisive and costly.

The means of grace

God has given ordinary means to strengthen believers: his word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, fellowship and worship. They are not magic, but they are how the Spirit normally works. A Christian who neglects them is fighting with no weapons.

“How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word. With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments! I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:9–11). Memorising and meditating on Scripture is one of the strongest weapons against temptation.

How are we sanctified?

Some teach that believers can reach sinless perfection in this life. Others teach a “higher life” of simple surrender — “let go and let God” — in which Christ lives the victorious life through you while you stop striving. Others stress human effort and discipline with little reference to grace.

Scripture teaches that sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). We work because God works. Perfection is never reached in this life (1 John 1:8), and passivity is never commanded; the New Testament is full of commands to put off, put to death, flee, strive and pursue.

And the fight involves both desires and habits. Behaviour change without heart change produces Pharisees. Heart change without new habits produces frustration. The Spirit works on both.

Is there anything in your life that feeds a sin you are fighting? What would it mean to make no provision for it?

For reflection

Why does the Bible use such violent language about sin? What does it mean to put sin to death “by the Spirit”? Choose a sin you are fighting: what should you put off, and what should you put on? Which means of grace do you most neglect, and how could you begin using it again?

5.title: Fighting Together
5.essay:
Many Christians fight sin alone, in secret. Ashamed to tell anyone, they confess privately to God, make private resolutions and fail privately again. Scripture calls us to a different path. The fight against sin is meant to be fought together.

Confess to one another

James pictures a praying community. The suffering pray, the cheerful sing, the sick call the elders. Then he widens it: “Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). Confession to God brings forgiveness. Confession to a trusted believer brings healing, accountability and prayer. Sin thrives in the dark. Brought into the light, it loses much of its power.

James says “to one another”, not to a priest who absolves sins. Every believer has direct access to God through Christ, and forgiveness comes from God alone. Confession to fellow believers is for mutual help and prayer.

It needs wisdom. Not every sin needs to be confessed to everyone. Sins against a particular person should be confessed to that person. Public sins may need public acknowledgment. Private struggles are best shared with a mature, trusted believer of the same sex.

Exhort one another daily

“But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). We need people who will ask us hard questions and speak truth to us. Sin is deceptive, and we are often the last to see our own.

When David sinned, God sent Nathan, who told him a story and then said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). David had hidden his sin for months. One faithful friend with a hard word brought him to repentance. “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy” (Proverbs 27:5–6). Flattery is easy and pleasant, but it leaves us in our sin.

Restore gently

“Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:1–2). When others confess to us, we must respond not with shock or gossip but with gentleness, prayer and practical help, remembering our own weakness. Yet “each will have to bear his own load” (Galatians 6:5). Mutual help does not remove personal responsibility.

Two are better than one

“Two are better than one … For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up! … a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12). Alone we are vulnerable; together we are strong.

And our company shapes us: “Do not be deceived: ‘Bad company ruins good morals’” (1 Corinthians 15:33). Those who want to grow in holiness should spend time with others who want the same.

The local church

God has placed believers in churches partly for this purpose. Elders watch over souls. Members encourage and warn one another. In serious cases, church discipline is a last resort to call a believer back from persistent sin. A Christian isolated from the church is far more vulnerable.

A church where everyone pretends to be fine will never become a place of healing. Leaders should model honesty about their own struggles, appropriately, so that others feel free to seek help.

Accountability that works

Good accountability is honest, regular and full of grace. It asks specific questions, prays together, celebrates progress, and responds to failure with the gospel rather than condemnation. It is not policing but brotherly love.

Three men in a church meet every other week for breakfast. They read Scripture, ask each other honest questions about their marriages, work and private lives, and pray. Over the years each has confessed sins he had never told anyone, and each has found help and prayer. None has been shamed.

Is there one person who knows your real struggles and regularly asks how you are doing?

For reflection

Why do Christians often fight sin alone, and what are the dangers? Who could you ask to be an accountability partner, and what questions would you want them to ask? How should you respond when someone confesses a sin to you? When has a friend’s hard word helped you?

6.title: When You Fall
6.essay:
Every believer will fall. The question is what we do next. Two responses are deadly: hiding the sin, and despairing of grace. Scripture shows a better way.

Come back quickly

“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2). John’s goal is that his readers not sin. But he knows they will, so he gives them the gospel. He does not say, “If anyone sins, he is lost.” He says we have an advocate. Jesus stands before the Father for us, and his sacrifice turns away God’s wrath. The believer who falls is not abandoned; he has the best possible defender. The way back is always open.

Confess honestly

Psalm 51, David’s prayer after his sin with Bathsheba, is the great model of repentance. He does not excuse or blame: “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned” (Psalm 51:3–4). He appeals to God’s mercy, not his own record: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love” (Psalm 51:1). He asks for cleansing, a clean heart and a right spirit. And he longs for joy: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). Repentance does not end in shame but in renewed joy.

Believe the forgiveness

After confession comes the part many find harder: believing that God has forgiven. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). God does not forgive grudgingly or in part. Do not keep punishing yourself for what Christ has paid for.

Godly grief

“For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). Worldly grief is sorry about the consequences, the embarrassment or the damage to our image. Godly grief is sorry for offending God, and it turns back to him.

Get up again

“For the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16). Seven times suggests many falls. The righteous are not those who never fall, but those who keep getting up by God’s grace. “Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise” (Micah 7:8). Perseverance, not perfection, is the mark of the godly.

Jesus prayed for Peter

Jesus knew Peter would deny him. He warned him, and prayed for him — not that Peter would not fall, but that his faith would not fail: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Jesus spoke of his restoration before the fall had even happened. After the resurrection he restored Peter publicly, and Peter’s fall became part of his ministry to others. Christ’s prayers keep his people through their failures.

Make amends, and learn

Where our sin has harmed others, repentance includes confessing to them and, where possible, making restitution. And after a fall, ask what led to it. What were the conditions? What lies did I believe? What practical steps can guard me next time? Repentance is not only sorrow for the past but a change of direction for the future.

A Christian who has been free from drinking for two years relapses after a bad week. His first instinct is to hide it and wallow in shame. Instead he calls his accountability partner that night, confesses, and they pray together. The next day he tells his wife. He reads Psalm 51 and 1 John 2:1–2. He is not proud of the fall, but he is not crushed by it. He gets up again.

Assurance and discipline

A true believer can fall seriously, as David and Peter did, and still be restored. But persistent, unrepentant sin is a warning sign. The answer to a fall is not to question every past experience but to repent and return. The Assurance of Salvation study explores this further.

God sometimes disciplines his children after a fall, through consequences or hardship. It is not punishment but training, a sign of his love: “For the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

When you sin, how long does it usually take before you confess it to God? What would help you come back more quickly?

For reflection

Read Psalm 51: which phrases could you pray after your own failures? What is the difference between godly and worldly grief? How does 1 John 2:1–2 give you hope when you sin? After a fall, what practical steps help you get up and guard against the next one?
